guided.title: Customers with repeat orders
guided.prompt: From `orders`, return `customer_id` and `orders` (the number of orders) for customers who placed at least 2 orders. Order by `orders` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.
guided.starter:
-- Customers with at least 2 orders
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY orders DESC, customer_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY orders DESC, customer_id;
hints: The starter lists every customer. The condition is about the size of each group, so it cannot go in WHERE.
HAVING goes after GROUP BY and before ORDER BY, and it can use an aggregate.

guided.title: Pricey categories
guided.prompt: From `products`, return `category_id`, `products` (how many products) and `avg_price` (average `unit_price` rounded to 2 decimals) for the categories whose average price is above 30. Order by `category_id` ascending.
guided.starter:
-- Categories whose average unit_price is above 30
SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS products, ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category_id
ORDER BY category_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS products, ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category_id
HAVING AVG(unit_price) > 30
ORDER BY category_id;
hints: The grouping and aggregates are already in the starter. Only the filter on the groups is missing.
The average per group exists after GROUP BY, so use HAVING, and repeat the aggregate expression.

guided.title: Shipped orders per carrier
guided.prompt: Count only the orders that have shipped (`shipped_date` is not NULL). Return `ship_via`, `orders` (count) and `total_freight` (sum of `freight`) for each carrier, ordered by `ship_via` ascending.
guided.starter:
-- Shipped orders and freight per carrier
SELECT ship_via, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(freight) AS total_freight
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_via
ORDER BY ship_via;
guided.solution:
SELECT ship_via, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(freight) AS total_freight
FROM orders
WHERE shipped_date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ship_via
ORDER BY ship_via;
hints: The starter counts all orders. The condition is about single rows, so it belongs before the grouping.
WHERE comes after FROM and before GROUP BY. Day 35 showed the NULL test for a missing date.

guided.title: Categories with many active products
guided.prompt: Ignore discontinued products (use `NOT discontinued`). Then return `category_id` and `active_products` (count) for categories that have at least 11 active products. Order by `category_id` ascending.
guided.starter:
-- Categories with at least 11 active products
SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS active_products
FROM products
WHERE NOT discontinued AND COUNT(*) >= 11
GROUP BY category_id
ORDER BY category_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS active_products
FROM products
WHERE NOT discontinued
GROUP BY category_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 11
ORDER BY category_id;
hints: Run the starter: PostgreSQL says aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE.
Split the two conditions: the discontinued flag is a row condition, the count is a group condition.
WHERE NOT discontinued ... GROUP BY category_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 11

independent.title: Busy cities
independent.prompt: From `customers`, return `country`, `city` and `customers` (the number of customers) for each country and city pair with at least 3 customers. Order by `customers` descending, then `country`, then `city`.
independent.starter:
-- Country and city pairs with at least 3 customers
SELECT country, city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY customers DESC, country, city;
independent.solution:
SELECT country, city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY country, city
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY customers DESC, country, city;

independent.title: Steady sellers
independent.prompt: From `order_details`, return for each product `product_id`, `lines` (number of order lines), `units` (sum of `quantity`) and `revenue` (sum of `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)` rounded to 2 decimals, with `discount` cast to `numeric`). Keep only products with at least 5 lines and at least 100 units. Order by `revenue` descending, then `product_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Products with at least 5 lines and 100 units
SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(quantity) AS units,
       ROUND(SUM(unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount::numeric)), 2) AS revenue
FROM order_details
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(quantity) AS units,
       ROUND(SUM(unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount::numeric)), 2) AS revenue
FROM order_details
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 AND SUM(quantity) >= 100
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id;

independent.title: Employees with expensive freight in 1997
independent.prompt: Stretch task. Using only orders placed in 1997 (1997-01-01 to 1997-12-31) and ignoring orders with no employee, return `employee_id`, `orders`, `total_freight` and `avg_freight` (rounded to 2 decimals) for employees with at least 10 such orders and an average freight above 80. Order by `employee_id`.
independent.starter:
-- 1997 orders per employee: at least 10 orders and average freight above 80
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(freight) AS total_freight,
       ROUND(AVG(freight), 2) AS avg_freight
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '1997-01-01' AND '1997-12-31'
GROUP BY employee_id
ORDER BY employee_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(freight) AS total_freight,
       ROUND(AVG(freight), 2) AS avg_freight
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '1997-01-01' AND '1997-12-31'
  AND employee_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY employee_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 AND AVG(freight) > 80
ORDER BY employee_id;

checks.question: You want the countries that have at least 5 orders. Where does the condition `COUNT(*) >= 5` go?
options: In WHERE, before GROUP BY
In HAVING, after GROUP BY
In ORDER BY
In the FROM clause
checks.explanation: The count of a group exists only after rows are grouped, and WHERE runs before grouping, so it cannot use aggregates. HAVING runs on the finished groups. ORDER BY only sorts and does not remove groups.

checks.question: One order has a NULL `employee_id`, and eight different employees have orders. How many rows does `SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY employee_id` return?
options: 8, because NULL is not a value
9, because all NULLs form one group
10, because the NULL row counts twice
It raises an error because of the NULL
checks.explanation: GROUP BY puts all NULLs in one group, so there are 8 employee groups plus one NULL group, 9 rows. It is not an error, and NULL rows are not dropped the way WHERE would drop them.

checks.question: Which statement fails?
options: SELECT ship_country, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY ship_country
SELECT ship_country, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY ship_country HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
SELECT ship_country, ship_via, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY ship_country
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY ship_country
checks.explanation: ship_via is neither a grouping column nor inside an aggregate, so one Germany group would need several ship_via values in one cell. PostgreSQL rejects it. The last query is valid: grouping columns need not be selected, though the result is hard to read.

checks.question: Which description matches `SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE unit_price > 20 GROUP BY category_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3`?
options: Count all products per category, then keep categories whose price is over 20
Keep products over 20, group them by category, then keep categories with more than 3 such products
Keep categories with more than 3 products, then keep products over 20
Group first, then count only products over 20 inside each category, keeping all categories
checks.explanation: The logical order is WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING. The count therefore only includes products priced over 20, and HAVING removes categories whose count of those products is 3 or less. The last option is wrong because categories with a count of 3 or less disappear.

checks.question: A query selects `COUNT(*) AS orders` and ends with `HAVING orders >= 5`. What happens in PostgreSQL?
options: It works, because HAVING can use any alias
It fails, because the alias does not exist yet when HAVING runs; write HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
It works only if the alias is in capital letters
It returns every group, because HAVING ignores aliases
checks.explanation: SELECT is evaluated after HAVING, so aliases defined in it are not visible. PostgreSQL reports that the column does not exist. ORDER BY comes after SELECT, which is why it can use aliases.

checks.question: Customers per country: Brazil 9, France 11, Germany 11, UK 7, USA 13, and every other country fewer than 7. How many rows does a query ending in `GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(*) >= 7` return?
options: All 21 countries
checks.explanation: Five countries have at least 7 customers: Brazil, France, Germany, UK and USA. HAVING removes the other countries entirely. The groups with exactly 7 count because the test is >=.
